flawed_step: The implication is false: vertex-deleted Hamiltonicity does not imply that the original graph is Hamiltonian.
counterexample: Use the Petersen graph with vertices a_i,b_i for i modulo 5 and edges a_i-a_{i+1}, a_i-b_i, and b_i-b_{i+2}. It is finite, simple, and connected. Deleting a_0 leaves the Hamiltonian cycle a_1-a_2-a_3-a_4-b_4-b_2-b_0-b_3-b_1-a_1. Deleting b_0 leaves the Hamiltonian cycle a_0-a_1-b_1-b_3-a_3-a_2-b_2-b_4-a_4-a_0. Rotating all indices modulo 5 gives a Hamiltonian cycle after deleting any a_i or any b_i. Yet the Petersen graph has no Hamiltonian cycle: such a cycle would cross the five-spoke cut an even number of times, hence use 2 or 4 spokes. With 2 spokes, their indices would need to be adjacent in the outer 5-cycle but differ by 2 in the inner 5-cycle, impossible. With 4 spokes, rotate so a_0-b_0 is omitted; the forced remaining edges split into the two disjoint cycles a_1-a_0-a_4-b_4-b_1-a_1 and a_2-a_3-b_3-b_0-b_2-a_2, not one Hamiltonian cycle.
assessment_summary: The Petersen graph is an explicit counterexample: every single-vertex deletion is Hamiltonian, while the graph itself is not.
